description: Added time compensates for time lost to injuries, goals and substitutions. Discover why stoppage time was invented in 1891 and how referees calculate it.

h1: Why Added Time Exists in Football
lead: A football match is 90 minutes — unless it is not. Added time, sometimes seven or ten minutes of it, is the referee's way of giving back the time the game lost. Here is why the rule exists and how it works.
thumbCaption: Why added time exists in football
share: Why do football matches have added time? It all started with a goalkeeper who kicked the ball out of the ground in 1891.
content:
Every football fan knows the drill: the fourth official holds up a board, the crowd groans, and play continues for another five, eight, even fourteen minutes. That period is called added time, stoppage time or injury time, and it exists for a surprisingly simple reason: football's clock does not stop when the ball goes out of play.

The Rule the Clock Forgot

Unlike American football or basketball, association football never stops the clock for throw-ins, goals, substitutions or injuries. A standard match is two halves of 45 minutes, played as one continuous 90-minute block. That design was fine when the game was slow, but it created an obvious loophole: a team losing by a goal could simply waste time until the final whistle.

Exactly that happened on 4 April 1891. Stoke City were awarded a last-minute penalty against Aston Villa, trailing 1-0. Villa's goalkeeper deliberately kicked the ball far out of the ground. By the time it was retrieved, the clock had expired and Stoke never took the penalty. The scandal was so blatant that the Football Association introduced added time for the 1891-92 season, and football has had stoppage time ever since.

Who Decides How Much Is Added?

There is no fixed formula. The referee is the sole timekeeper and decides how many minutes to add at the end of each half, based on time lost to:

  • Substitutions — each one typically costs around 30 seconds
  • Injuries requiring treatment on the pitch
  • Goals and extended goal celebrations
  • Yellow and red cards and the resulting delays
  • VAR reviews
  • Cooling or drinks breaks in hot weather
Key point: The minutes shown on the board are a minimum. The referee can add more time within the added time itself if further stoppages occur — which is why games sometimes seem to drift past the number on the board.

The Rise of Big Added-Time Numbers

In the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, added time suddenly became a talking point after FIFA told referees to more accurately account for stoppages. The tournament produced some of the longest added-time periods ever recorded, including 14 minutes added at the end of the first half in England's group game against Iran after a serious head injury to the Iranian goalkeeper. For comparison, stoppage time of four or five minutes was the norm in earlier decades.

Why Effective Playing Time Is So Low

Here is the surprising fact behind the rule: a 90-minute match contains roughly one hour of actual playing time. The rest — around 30 minutes — is lost to throw-ins, free kicks, goal kicks, corners, injuries and the ball rolling out of play. Added time does not fully compensate for that lost time; it only compensates for the stoppages the referee judges to be 'wasted'.

Cooling Breaks and the Weather Clause

In extreme heat, referees can also stop the game for cooling breaks after the 30th minute of each half when conditions get dangerously hot, with the lost minutes added on at the end of the half. That is why matches played in summer tournaments often show unusually high added-time figures.

Why Not Just Stop the Clock?

Critics regularly ask why football does not simply pause the clock like other sports. The answer is tradition and flow: football's continuous clock is part of what gives the sport its rhythm, and stopping it for every throw-in would add 30 to 40 minutes to every broadcast. Instead, the game accepts a small inaccuracy at the end of each half — and accepts that the referee, not the clock, has the final say.

Added time has produced some of the most dramatic moments in the sport's history, from last-minute winners to stoppage-time title twists. For a deeper look at how those late minutes behave, see our analysis of stoppage-time goals and patterns.

h1: Why Football Matches Go to Extra Time
lead: When a knockout tie is level after 90 minutes, football does not decide it by chance. It plays another 30 minutes first. Here is why extra time exists — and why it has almost been abolished twice.
thumbCaption: Why football matches go to extra time
share: Two extra 15-minute halves, the golden goal era and the first penalty shootout in 1976 — how football settles drawn knockout ties.
content:
In a league match, a draw is a perfectly good result. In a cup tie or a tournament final, someone has to win. Football's answer is a 30-minute extension of the game called extra time, and if that fails, the penalty shootout. But the rules have changed dramatically over the decades — and at times, the entire concept has been on the verge of disappearing.

What Extra Time Actually Is

When a knockout match is tied after 90 minutes, the game continues with two periods of 15 minutes each, with a brief interval to swap ends. Goals scored in extra time count towards the final score. If the score is still level after 120 minutes, the match goes to a penalty shootout.

One extra thing: Teams also gain a sixth substitute for extra time in most competitions, which can completely change how a tired team approaches the extra half hour.

Why 30 Minutes?

There is no grand mathematical reason for 30 minutes. It simply evolved as a practical extension — short enough to be survivable, long enough to give one side a genuine chance to win on merit. Some competitions, like the old FA Cup, originally resolved draws with replays instead, with extra time and shootouts reserved for later rounds.

The Golden Goal Experiment

In 1993, FIFA tried to make extra time more exciting by introducing the golden goal: the first team to score in extra time won the match immediately. It was designed to reward attacking play and avoid the 'both teams sitting back' criticism of the old format.

The first golden goal at a World Cup was Laurent Blanc's winner for France against Paraguay in 1998. Germany's Oliver Bierhoff scored the most famous one — a golden goal to win Euro 96 against the Czech Republic. But the format had a flaw: teams became even more cautious, terrified of conceding the killer goal. FIFA scrapped the golden goal in 2004 after trying the silver goal — where the leading team after the first 15-minute period won — for only two years.

The Penalty Shootout: Football's Most Dramatic Ending

When extra time does not settle a tie, football turns to the penalty shootout. The format was formally adopted by FIFA in 1970, and its first use at a major international tournament was the 1976 European Championship final, when Czechoslovakia beat West Germany 5-3 on penalties after a 2-2 draw. The winning kick was Antonin Panenka's infamous slow chip straight down the middle — the original 'Panenka', still imitated by every showman since.

The shootout reached the World Cup for the first time in 1982, and has produced some of the most traumatic and glorious moments in the sport — from Baggio's miss in 1994 to Grobbelaar's spaghetti legs in 1984.

Why Some Competitions Skip Extra Time

Not every competition uses extra time. The English League Cup abolished extra time in the early rounds in 2018, sending drawn ties straight to penalties after 90 minutes to reduce fixture congestion. Some youth tournaments and pre-season friendlies skip it for the same reason. There have also been recurring proposals to remove extra time from major tournaments entirely, with one idea — straight to penalties after 90 minutes — gaining support because 120 minutes of football has been linked to player fatigue and injury risk.

FormatWhen usedStatus
Two x 15-min periodsStandard knockout footballCurrent rule
Golden goal1993-2004 (most FIFA competitions)Abolished
Silver goal2002-2004Abolished
Straight to penaltiesEFL Cup early roundsUsed in some competitions

Extra time has survived every reform attempt because it preserves football's most fundamental promise: the team that plays better over a longer period deserves the win. And when 120 minutes cannot separate two sides, the shootout — controversial, beloved and hated — settles the argument in the most dramatic way the sport knows.

description: Shirt swapping began with a 1931 France-England friendly and exploded after Pelé and Moore. Why footballers exchange shirts — and the rule crackdown.
keywords: why footballers exchange shirts, shirt swap football, shirt swapping tradition, Pele Moore shirt swap, shirt exchange rule, football shirt swap yellow card
h1: Why Footballers Exchange Shirts After Matches
lead: It is the last ritual of every big match: two players swap sweaty shirts and head to the tunnel. Shirt exchanges are football's oldest gesture of respect — and now they come with a warning.
thumbCaption: Why footballers exchange shirts after matches
share: From a 1931 friendly to Pelé and Bobby Moore — the story of why footballers exchange shirts.
content:
After the final whistle, when the handshakes are done and the cameras are watching, the shirt exchange happens. Two players — usually opponents who have spent ninety minutes trying to destroy each other — peel off their match jerseys and swap them as a token of mutual respect. It is one of football's most recognisable images, and it has a surprisingly long history.

Where the Tradition Began

The earliest recorded shirt swap took place on 14 May 1931, when France beat England 5-2 in a friendly near Paris. According to the match reports of the day, the two sides exchanged shirts as a gesture of sportsmanship at full-time. It was an isolated incident, though — for decades, the swap was rare enough that it made the news every time it happened.

The Moment That Made It Famous

The tradition became iconic at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico. After England's group-stage defeat to Brazil, captain Bobby Moore and Pelé — the two most respected players of the era — swapped shirts on the pitch. The image of Moore and Pelé in each other's jerseys was beamed around the world and became a symbol of the game's gentlemanly spirit. From that moment, shirt exchanges went from a rarity to a rite of passage.

Why Do Players Do It?

There are several reasons, and they have shifted over time:

  • Respect — exchanging shirts honours an opponent who played well or a player you idolise.
  • Memorabilia — match-worn shirts of legends are valuable collector's items, and players build collections of their own.
  • Goodwill — in football's early days, players simply could not afford to buy shirts, so swapping was also a practical exchange.
  • Tradition — young players want to emulate the stars they watched growing up.

The Famous Swaps

Some swaps have become part of football folklore. The most sought-after is a swap with Lionel Messi or Cristiano Ronaldo, whose match shirts sell at auction for tens of thousands of pounds. Pelé's 1970 World Cup final shirt sold for over £150,000 decades later. For elite players, collecting the shirt of a respected rival is the modern equivalent of a medal you can keep privately.

The Modern Rule Crackdown

In recent years, the shirt exchange has collided with football's time-wasting rules. Officials have been told to treat shirt swaps before full-time as deliberate time-wasting, and football's rulemakers confirmed in 2023 that players who exchange shirts at half-time — when both teams are leaving the pitch and the swap delays the restart — will be cautioned with a yellow card. The rule does not ban the tradition; it simply ensures that a player who wants a shirt waits until the match is properly over.

The etiquette: The proper way to swap is after the final whistle, on the pitch, with a handshake. The half-time swap, however iconic it looks, is now officially a booking offence.

Is the Tradition Dying?

Far from it. Despite the rule clarification, shirt exchanges are as common as ever — and the list of players lining up for a jersey after the final whistle has become part of every big match broadcast. The tradition has simply adapted: swap on the field, at full-time, and keep the souvenir for the collection. As long as players respect each other, the shirt swap will survive.

h1: Why Fans Call It Football or Soccer
lead: Same sport, two names. 'Football' and 'soccer' both come from England — and the word Americans use was actually invented by British university students.
thumbCaption: Why it is called football or soccer
share: Soccer is a British invention. Here is how the same sport ended up with two names around the world.
content:
To a British fan, the sport is football, full stop. To an American, it is soccer. Both sides have argued about it for decades, and both are using the same word — because 'soccer' was coined in England, not America, and was in everyday use there long before it crossed the Atlantic.

The Name Came From the Rules

In the 1860s, as different versions of football were being standardised in English public schools, the two dominant codes were distinguished by their governing bodies. The game played under Football Association rules was officially called association football, while the rival code, played under the rules of the Rugby Football Union, was rugby football — or simply 'rugger'.

The Oxford Slang That Made 'Soccer'

Around 1875, university students in Oxford and Cambridge developed a playful slang habit of adding '-er' to words. 'Association football' became assoccer, shortened to soccer. The earliest recorded spellings ran from 'socca' in 1889 and 'socker' in 1891 to the modern 'soccer' by 1895. The same slang produced 'rugger' for rugby — which is still used today — and oddities like 'footer' for association football.

The word 'soccer' was never American slang. It was British university slang that spread through the British press, and it was used interchangeably with 'football' in England well into the twentieth century.

Why America Kept 'Soccer'

When association football spread to the United States around the early 1900s, Americans already had a sport called football: American football, which had evolved from rugby. To avoid confusion, the version played with the round ball was branded 'soccer' — the English word that distinguished it from gridiron.

Then a second factor locked the name in. In the 1960s and 70s, the sport's professional league in America adopted 'soccer' as its official identity — the North American Soccer League, then Major League Soccer. The word became part of the sport's American brand, and despite periodic campaigns to call it football, 'soccer' remains the standard in the United States, Canada, Australia and South Africa.

A World Divided

Today the usage looks like this:

CountryNameWhy
United KingdomFootballThe original name, from 'foot' + 'ball'
United States & CanadaSoccerTo distinguish it from gridiron
AustraliaSoccerTo distinguish it from Australian rules and rugby
South AfricaSoccerHistorically used alongside rugby culture
Most of Europe & Latin AmericaFootball / fútbol / calcioLocal translations of the same word

The Great Debate of the 2000s

In the 2000s, 'soccer' became a fighting word. English fans accused Americans of 'stealing' the name of their sport, while American fans pointed out — correctly — that the word was invented in Britain. The FA's own history confirms that 'soccer' was English slang long before it was American, and even FIFA's official name for the sport is 'association football'.

Final answer: Both words are correct. Football is the sport's true name; soccer is a British abbreviation that the rest of the English-speaking world kept, even as Britain itself abandoned it.

If there is a football lesson in the argument, it is this: football's rules were standardised in England, but its language is global. For more on how the modern game took shape, see the origin of the offside rule and the history of the red and yellow cards.
